verses.context: The beast and the false prophet have been thrown into the lake of fire (19:20). One enemy remains, the dragon, and an unnamed angel comes down equipped to deal with him. The verse sets the scene with two objects: a key and a chain.
verses.grammar: Eidon, ‘I saw’, opens the first of three visions in the chapter (verses 1, 4, and 11). Katabainonta, ‘coming down’, is a present participle, the same description given to the mighty angel of 10:1 and the angel of 18:1. The angel holds tēn klein tēs abussou, ‘the key of the Abyss’, and halusin megalēn, ‘a great chain’. The key of the Abyss was given to a fallen star in 9:1 to release the locusts; now it is used to lock the Abyss's chief prisoner in. The risen Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (1:18), so every key in the book is finally in God's hands.
verses.history: Jewish writings before Revelation already pictured rebel angels bound and imprisoned until the judgment. In 1 Enoch 10:4-6, God tells the angel Raphael to bind Azazel hand and foot and cast him into darkness, covering him with rough stones until the great day of judgment. 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 reflect the same tradition. Revelation's binding of the devil draws on this shared picture.

ot.note: In Isaiah's vision of the end, the LORD punishes the host of heaven on high and the kings of the earth below; they are gathered as prisoners in a pit, shut up in a prison, and ‘after many days’ they will be punished. The Septuagint speaks of them being shut in a fortress and a prison. The pattern of imprisonment first and final punishment later is exactly the pattern of Revelation 20:1-10, and many commentators see this passage behind it.

verses.context: The angel seizes the dragon, binds him, throws him into the Abyss, and seals it for a thousand years. The purpose is stated precisely: so that he could not deceive the nations. Then comes an ominous necessity: he must be released for a little while.
verses.grammar: The dragon is named with the full set of titles from 12:9, and the Greek shifts case to do it: ton drakonta (accusative, the object of ‘seized’) is followed by ho ophis ho archaios (nominative), a characteristic feature of Revelation's style in which a title keeps its fixed form regardless of the grammar around it (compare 1:4). Four aorists follow in quick succession (ekratēsen, edēsen, ebalen, ekleisen) and a fifth, esphragisen, ‘sealed’. The purpose clause is narrow: hina mē planēsē eti ta ethnē, ‘so that he might no longer deceive the nations’. What is restricted is one activity, deceiving the nations. Dei luthēnai, ‘it is necessary that he be released’, uses dei, the word Revelation uses for what God's plan requires (1:1, 4:1).
verses.history: The literal reading of the thousand years is the oldest one on record. Papias of Hierapolis, early in the second century, taught a coming earthly kingdom of extraordinary abundance, as Irenaeus reports (Against Heresies 5.33.3-4); Eusebius (Church History 3.39.12-13) preserved the report while judging Papias a man of limited understanding for it. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 80-81, around AD 155-160) expected a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem, cited John's Revelation by name, and admitted that some true Christians thought otherwise. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.32-36, around 180) argued at length that the promises to Abraham require an earthly kingdom of the righteous before the final judgment. In the third century Dionysius of Alexandria answered the millenarian bishop Nepos in a debate Eusebius records (Church History 7.24-25).

theology.note: A single angel, not Christ himself, is enough to bind the devil, and the devil's release happens because it ‘must’, by God's appointment. Nothing in the passage gives the dragon an initiative of his own.

Amillennial and postmillennial readers connect this binding with Jesus' saying about binding the strong man (Mark 3:27) and with his casting out of the ruler of this world at the cross (John 12:31): Satan is restrained now so that he cannot keep the nations from hearing the gospel. Premillennial readers note that the New Testament still describes Satan as actively deceiving (2 Corinthians 4:4; 1 Peter 5:8) and expect a fuller binding after Christ's return.

verses.context: The second vision: thrones, judges, and the souls of the faithful who had died for Jesus or refused the beast. They come to life and reign with Christ for the thousand years. What the beast took from them in chapter 13 is reversed here.
verses.grammar: Krima edothē autois, literally ‘judgment was given to them’, echoes Daniel 7:22, where judgment is given for the holy ones; it can mean they are vindicated or that they are given authority to judge, and Revelation probably intends both. Psuchas, ‘souls’, recalls the souls under the altar in 6:9. Pepelekismenōn, a perfect passive participle, means ‘beheaded’, literally ‘axed’, from pelekus, an axe. The decisive verb is ezēsan: ‘they lived’ or ‘they came to life’. As an ingressive aorist (an aorist that marks the entry into a state) it means ‘came to life’, which is how the BSB takes it, and Revelation uses the same form of Christ's resurrection in 2:8. Whether it means bodily resurrection here is the center of the millennial debate.
verses.history: Tyconius, a Donatist lay theologian in North Africa, wrote a commentary on Revelation around 380 that is now lost but whose readings survive in later writers; he read the book's visions as describing the church's present life, not a future timetable. Augustine adopted this approach in The City of God (20.7-9, written in the 420s), confessing that he had once held a millenarian view. He took the first resurrection as the soul's rising to new life in Christ, the binding of Satan as his restraint from seducing the church, and the reign of the saints as the church's present rule with Christ, including the faithful departed. His reading shaped Western interpretation for a thousand years. In the twelfth century Joachim of Fiore (died 1202) broke with it by expecting a coming age of the Holy Spirit within history, and some of his later followers fixed its date by the 1,260 days of Revelation 12:6. The Lutheran Augsburg Confession (1530, Article 17) rejected the teaching that the godly will rule an earthly kingdom before the resurrection of the dead.

theology.note: Amillennial readers see in this verse the state of believers between death and resurrection: the souls of the martyrs are alive with Christ and share his reign now, while their bodies wait for the resurrection at the end. On this reading the verse answers the cry of 6:9-11 by showing the martyrs already enthroned.

Premillennial readers take ‘came to life’ as bodily resurrection at Christ's return, the same kind of event as the resurrection of ‘the rest of the dead’ in verse 5, which they place a thousand years later. Either way, the verse insists that those the beast killed are not finally dead.

ot.note: In Daniel's Aramaic, thrones are set in place and the Ancient of Days takes his seat; in 7:22 judgment is given for the holy ones of the Most High and the time comes for them to possess the kingdom, and 7:27 gives the kingdom to the people of the holy ones. Theodotion's Greek of 7:22 reads to krima edōken hagiois. John's scene follows the Daniel sequence: thrones, judgment given, and the saints' reign after the beast's defeat.

verses.context: The verse makes a contrast (the rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years ended) and then names what verse 4 described: "This is the first resurrection." The phrase implies a second, though the text never uses that expression.
verses.grammar: Ouk ezēsan, ‘did not live’ or ‘did not come to life’, repeats the verb of verse 4. Henry Alford, in his nineteenth-century Greek Testament, argued that if the same word in the same passage means spiritual life in one verse and bodily resurrection in the next, the passage cannot be read consistently; that argument remains the premillennial reading's strongest point. Amillennial scholars answer that the passage itself sets up an asymmetry, a first resurrection matched by a second death, so the first of each pair need not be the same kind of event as the second. Meredith Kline made this case in an article titled The First Resurrection (Westminster Theological Journal, 1975). Hautē hē anastasis hē prōtē, ‘this is the first resurrection’, uses anastasis, the ordinary New Testament word for resurrection, which is itself part of the debate.
verses.text: The first sentence of the verse, about the rest of the dead, is missing from Codex Sinaiticus and from some Syriac manuscripts. Verses 4 and 5 both end with ‘the thousand years’, so a copyist's eye could easily jump from one to the other; the sentence is in Codex Alexandrinus and the great majority of manuscripts, and every modern edition keeps it.

theology.note: John 5:24-29 speaks of two ‘hours’: one that ‘now is’, when the spiritually dead hear the Son's voice and live, and one that is coming, when all in the tombs will come out. Amillennial readers find the same two stages here; premillennial readers see two bodily resurrections separated by the millennium. Both read the verse as a promise that death does not have the last word over the faithful.

verses.history: The modern positions took shape after the Reformation. Postmillennialism, argued by the Anglican Daniel Whitby (1703) and embraced by Jonathan Edwards and many nineteenth-century evangelicals, reads the thousand years as a long future era, not necessarily a literal thousand, in which the gospel's spread brings much of the world under Christ's rule before he returns; Loraine Boettner restated it in The Millennium (1957). Dispensational premillennialism grew from the teaching of John Nelson Darby among the Plymouth Brethren from the 1830s and spread through the Scofield Reference Bible (1909); it reads the thousand years as a literal reign of Christ from Jerusalem in which God's promises to national Israel are fulfilled, usually after the church has been taken up before a seven-year tribulation, and John Walvoord's The Millennial Kingdom (1959) is a standard statement. Historic premillennialism, defended by George Eldon Ladd, keeps the order of Christ's return, a bodily first resurrection, and an earthly reign, without the dispensational distinction between Israel and the church or a rapture before the tribulation. Amillennialism, set out by Anthony Hoekema in The Bible and the Future (1979), follows Augustine in reading the thousand years as the present age. Ladd and Hoekema, with Loraine Boettner and the dispensationalist Herman Hoyt, argued the four positions face to face in The Meaning of the Millennium: Four Views, edited by Robert Clouse (1977).

verses.context: The fifth of Revelation's seven beatitudes pronounces those in the first resurrection blessed and holy. Three things follow: the second death has no power over them, they will be priests, and they will reign with Christ.
verses.grammar: Makarios kai hagios, ‘blessed and holy’, is the only beatitude in the book with a second adjective. Ho echōn meros en tē anastasei, ‘the one who has a share in the resurrection’, uses meros, a portion or inheritance, the word Jesus used when he told Peter ‘you have no part with me’ (John 13:8). Epi toutōn ho deuteros thanatos ouk echei exousian, ‘over these the second death has no authority’: exousia is the word used all through chapter 13 for the beast's granted power, and here death itself is denied it. The futures esontai and basileusousin, ‘they will be’ and ‘they will reign’, look ahead through the thousand years.
verses.history: The phrase ‘second death’ appears in the Aramaic Targums, the translations and paraphrases of Scripture read in synagogues. Targum Onqelos on Deuteronomy 33:6 renders Moses' blessing ‘Let Reuben live and not die’ as a prayer that Reuben live in eternal life and not die the second death. Revelation uses the phrase four times (2:11, 20:6, 20:14, 21:8), always for final exclusion from God's life.

theology.note: The promise is not simply survival but vocation: the faithful will serve as priests and reign. The hope held out to martyrs is a restored human calling, the priestly rule given to Israel at Sinai and to humanity at creation.

ot.note: At Sinai God tells Israel that they will be to him mamlekhet kohanim, ‘a kingdom of priests’, and a holy nation; the Septuagint renders it basileion hierateuma, ‘a royal priesthood’. Revelation has already applied this to the church in 1:6 and 5:10, and here it becomes the reward of the first resurrection. Isaiah 61:6 had promised that the restored people would be called priests of the LORD.

verses.context: When the thousand years end, Satan is released and does again what he was prevented from doing: he deceives the nations and gathers them for war. The names Gog and Magog tie this last rebellion to Ezekiel's prophecy.
verses.grammar: The verbs shift from the past tense of the visions to the future: luthēsetai, ‘will be released’, and exeleusetai, ‘will go out’. John is now foretelling rather than reporting what he saw. The purpose, planēsai ta ethnē, ‘to deceive the nations’, repeats verse 3 exactly: the restraint is lifted and the old work resumes. Sunagagein autous eis ton polemon, ‘to gather them for the battle’, uses the article, ‘the battle’, and the same phrase occurs in 16:14 and 19:19. R. Fowler White, in a 1989 study in the Westminster Theological Journal, argued that the repeated phrase and the shared use of Ezekiel 38-39 in 19:17-21 and 20:7-10 show these are one battle told twice, which supports the amillennial reading of chapter 20 as a new view of the same history. Premillennial readers answer that 20:7-10 comes explicitly after the thousand years, so it cannot be the battle of 19:19.
verses.history: In Genesis 10:2 Magog is one of the sons of Japheth, the ancestor of northern peoples, and Josephus (Antiquities 1.123) identifies the Magogians with the people the Greeks called Scythians. In Ezekiel, Gog is the ruler and Magog his land. Revelation turns both names into a description of the nations from the four corners of the earth, humanity as a whole in rebellion.

theology.note: After a long age without the devil's deception of the nations, the nations still follow him when he is released. Whatever the thousand years are, the verses show that human rebellion is not cured by a better environment; the heart must be made new.

ot.note: Ezekiel is told to set his face toward Gog, of the land of Magog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, who will lead a vast coalition against God's restored people living securely, and God will destroy him (chapters 38 and 39). In the Hebrew, Magog is a land; the Septuagint keeps it as a place name. Ezekiel's attack comes after Israel's restoration and the gift of God's Spirit (chapters 36 and 37), which is why premillennial readers see a fitting parallel in an attack after the thousand years, while amillennial readers note that 19:17-21 also draws on Ezekiel 39.

verses.context: The nations surround God's people, and fire from heaven ends the rebellion without a battle. The saints do nothing; God acts.
verses.grammar: Anebēsan epi to platos tēs gēs, ‘they went up over the breadth of the earth’, echoes Habakkuk 1:6, where the Babylonians march through the breadth of the earth. Tēn parembolēn tōn hagiōn, ‘the camp of the saints’: parembolē is the Septuagint's regular word for Israel's camp in the wilderness (Numbers 2 and elsewhere), so God's people are pictured as still on the march toward their inheritance. Tēn polin tēn ēgapēmenēn, ‘the beloved city’, uses a perfect passive participle of agapaō: the city that has been and remains loved. Katephagen autous, ‘devoured them’, is the verb used of the dragon's intent toward the child in 12:4.
verses.text: Some manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read that fire came down ‘from God out of heaven’. The shorter reading, ‘from heaven’, is supported by Codex Alexandrinus and is printed by modern editions; the longer one may have been expanded from 21:2 and 21:10. The meaning does not change.

theology.note: The final rebellion is ended by God's direct act, as Ezekiel promised (38:22, 39:6). The verse gives no role to human armies on either side: judgment belongs to God.

ot.note: God tells Gog that he will judge him with plague and bloodshed, torrential rain, hailstones, and fire and sulfur; Ezekiel 39:6 adds that he will send fire on Magog. The Septuagint of both verses uses pur, ‘fire’. Revelation combines this with the fire from heaven that consumed the soldiers sent against Elijah (2 Kings 1:10-12), so Gog's army meets the end God had promised.

verses.context: The devil joins the beast and the false prophet in the lake of fire, and the three are tormented forever. The enemy introduced in chapter 12 is now finished.
verses.grammar: Ho planōn autous, ‘the one deceiving them’, is a present participle used as a title, as in 12:9: deception is his identity. Eblēthē, ‘was thrown’, is the same verb used for his fall from heaven (12:9); this is the last throwing. Basanisthēsontai, ‘they will be tormented’, is a future passive of basanizō. Eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn, ‘into the ages of the ages’, is the strongest phrase Greek has for unending time; Revelation uses it of God's life (4:9-10) and of Christ's reign (11:15). The subject of the verb is plural: the devil, the beast, and the false prophet.
verses.history: Sulfur, theion, was associated with divine judgment from the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24), and volcanic sulfur springs were known around the eastern Mediterranean. The Dead Sea region, where the Sodom tradition was located, is rich in sulfur deposits, and Josephus (Jewish War 4.476-485) describes the region's bitumen and the traces of Sodom's burning still visible in his day. John's image draws on the Sodom story and on Isaiah 34:9-10, where the land of Edom becomes burning sulfur and its smoke goes up forever.

theology.note: The traditional reading of the lake of fire as unending conscious punishment leans heavily on this verse. Conditionalist readers, among them Edward Fudge and John Stott, reply that the torment here is said of the devil and two symbolic figures, the beast and the false prophet, which stand for systems rather than individual people, and that the lake is defined in verse 14 as ‘the second death’. Traditionalists answer that 14:10-11 uses the same language of human beings who worship the beast.

verses.context: The third vision: a great white throne and the one seated on it, before whom earth and heaven flee. The old creation gives way before the judge, clearing the stage for the new heaven and earth of 21:1.
verses.grammar: Thronon megan leukon, ‘a great white throne’: megas speaks of majesty and leukos of purity, the white of the risen Christ's hair and garments (1:14) and of the faithful's robes (7:9). Ephugen, ‘fled’, is singular with a double subject, earth and heaven, treating them as one thing. Topos ouch heurethē autois, ‘no place was found for them’, repeats 12:8 and echoes Theodotion's Greek of Daniel 2:35, where the image of the kingdoms is struck by the stone and ‘no place was found for them’. The one seated on the throne is not named; elsewhere Revelation seats God on the throne (4:2) and later speaks of ‘the throne of God and of the Lamb’ (22:1).

theology.note: The judge's presence alone dissolves the world as it is. The New Testament elsewhere says that the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22) and that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), so the church has read this throne as the throne of God shared with the Lamb.

ot.note: Daniel sees thrones set, the Ancient of Days seated in garments white as snow, a river of fire flowing from before him, and the court sitting with the books opened. The Septuagint and Theodotion both have biblous ēneōchthēsan, ‘books were opened’. John follows this sequence in verses 11 and 12: a throne, whiteness, the court, and opened books.

verses.context: All the dead stand before the throne, and books are opened: records of deeds and the Book of Life. The judgment is by works, and the Book of Life stands beside them as a separate book.
verses.grammar: Tous megalous kai tous mikrous, ‘the great and the small’, reverses the order used of the beast's subjects in 13:16 and includes everyone. Hestōtas, a perfect participle, ‘standing’, pictures them in place before the court. Biblia ēnoichthēsan, ‘books were opened’, then allo biblion, ‘another book’, the book of life: two kinds of record, one of deeds and one of names. Ekrithēsan ... ek tōn gegrammenōn en tois bibliois kata ta erga autōn, ‘they were judged out of the things written in the books, according to their works’: the preposition ek names the evidence and kata the standard.
verses.history: The idea of heavenly books was familiar in Jewish thought. Malachi 3:16 speaks of a book of remembrance written before the LORD, and the Mishnah (m. Avot 2:1) teaches that a person should remember that an eye sees, an ear hears, and all their deeds are written in a book. Daniel 12:1 speaks of those whose names are written in the book being delivered.
verses.text: Where modern editions read that the dead stood ‘before the throne’, later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘before God’. The older reading keeps the focus on the throne of verse 11.

theology.note: The books of deeds and the Book of Life stand side by side. Deeds are real evidence, and no one is judged on anything else; yet 21:27 calls the Book of Life the Lamb's, and 13:8 says the names were written there before the beast demanded worship. The verse holds together judgment by works and rescue by grace, as Paul does in Romans 2:6 and 3:23-24.

verses.context: No one is missing. The sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead, and each person is judged individually by what they have done.
verses.grammar: Edōken hē thalassa tous nekrous, ‘the sea gave the dead’: the sea, Death, and Hades are personified as holders who must hand over what they hold. The verb is edōken, ‘gave’, the verb used through chapter 13 for what was granted to the beast; here the great powers of death are forced to give. Ekrithēsan hekastos, ‘they were judged, each one’, has a plural verb with a singular subject: the judgment is collective in scene and individual in substance.

theology.note: The verse assumes a general resurrection: those lost at sea, with no grave, and those held by Death and Hades are all restored to stand before God. The church's creeds confess the same, the resurrection of the dead and the judgment of the living and the dead.

verses.context: Death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire. What has held the dead is destroyed, and the lake is given its name: the second death.
verses.grammar: Ho thanatos kai ho hadēs eblēthēsan, ‘Death and Hades were thrown’: the two appear as a pair throughout the book (1:18, 6:8), and now they share the fate of the devil. Houtos ho thanatos ho deuteros estin, hē limnē tou puros, ‘this is the second death, the lake of fire’: the final phrase stands in apposition and defines the one by the other. The definition matters for the debate over the lake's meaning, since ‘death’ is the Bible's usual word for the end of life, not for its continuation.
verses.text: The closing words ‘the lake of fire’ are missing from the manuscripts behind the King James Version, which ends the verse ‘This is the second death’. The earlier manuscripts include them, and modern editions print them.

theology.note: Death is not only defeated but abolished. The verse prepares for 21:4, where there is no more death, and fulfills Paul's promise that the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26).

ot.note: Isaiah promises that on the mountain of the LORD, God will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces. The Hebrew billa hammavet lanetsach reads ‘he will swallow up death forever’; the Septuagint turns it into ‘death, having prevailed, swallowed up’, and Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:54 uses a form closer to the Hebrew. Revelation depicts the promise being carried out here and quotes the tears line in 21:4.

verses.context: The chapter ends with the decisive criterion: whoever is not found written in the Book of Life is thrown into the lake of fire. After a chapter of cosmic enemies, the last verse concerns ‘anyone’.
verses.grammar: Ei tis ouch heurethē ... gegrammenos, ‘if anyone was not found written’, is a simple condition stated as a fact about the past from the standpoint of the vision. Heurethē, ‘was found’, is the verb of 12:8 and 20:11, where no place was found for the dragon and for the old heaven and earth; here the search is for a name. Gegrammenos is a perfect passive participle, ‘having been written and remaining so’, the same perfect used in 13:8 of the names written in the Lamb's book.
verses.history: The lake of fire has been read three main ways. The church's majority tradition, from Augustine (The City of God, book 21) through Thomas Aquinas and Jonathan Edwards, holds that it means unending conscious punishment. Conditional immortality, argued by Edward Fudge in The Fire That Consumes (1982) and tentatively by John Stott in Essentials (1988), holds that the second death is final destruction. A hope for universal restoration goes back to Origen and Gregory of Nyssa; Origenist teaching on the restoration of all things was condemned in anathemas associated with the Second Council of Constantinople (553), and the view has had modern defenders such as Robin Parry. The creeds confess judgment without defining the lake's nature, and all three readings take the verse's warning seriously.

theology.note: The verse makes exclusion from the Book of Life the ground of final judgment. It speaks of the lake as the destination of those not written, without describing their state there, which is why readers who agree on the warning still differ on its nature.

The last word of the chapter rests on a book the Lamb holds. The warning is severe, but its point for John's hearers is assurance: those written in the Lamb's book do not share the fate of the dragon and his beasts.
